newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH RATE RISE ALREADY DISCOUNTED BY MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH RATE RISE ALREADY DISCOUNTED BY MARKETS.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland's (NBP) widely anticipated official interest rise was already mostly discounted by Poland's financial markets, analysts said.
Earlier today the central bank said it would on August 4 increase the lombard rate by two points to 27 percent and the discount rate by 2.5 points to 24.5 percent, as expected.

The reaction of the volatile forex market to the rate hike remained as the only question mark, which analysts said may have been the reason behind the central banker's statement that the zloty had some room to rise after rates were increased.
"The zloty should get a boost from the rate rise. It may push the local unit back above the parity rate," said Piotr Czyzewski, dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.

But others said, however, that large foreign investor entry into Polish T-bills was needed to sustain zloty gains and that such inflows were not expected before parliamentary elections in late September.

On Friday the zloty gained nearly half a point on interest rate rise expectations to close at minus 0.87 percent from parity, against Thursday's minus 1.27 percent and last week's close at minus 0.81 percent.
It closed at 3.4660 per dollar and at 1.8720 to the mark.
Analysts said the Warsaw bourse could fall early next week after the interest rate rise but they saw the market's downside capped because the news had already been largely priced in.
"The market could fall a little on Monday, but not too much, because to a large degree this has been discounted," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital & Investment.
The main market's all-share WIG index rose 0.4 percent this week to 15,116.8 points, but the outlook remained rather grim.
Analysts said the index was bound to drift downward before parliamentary polls, deflated further by the recent flood, which devestated large chunks of southern and western Poland.
Poland's debt market also already weighed in the rate hike, which was preceeded by several weeks of market rates increases and more than two months of growing T-bill yields.
"The market had already discounted such a rate rise so treasury yields at primary tenders are not likely to go much higher," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski of ING Bank in Warsaw.

Dealers said the finance ministry could afford to cap yield growth through its new 2.5 billion zloty credit line from the NBP, written into the 1997 budget last month in order to help Poland maintain liquidity amid mounting flood relief costs.

"The interest rate rise should not have a large effect on T-bill yields because the finance ministry now has an air-bag in the form of additional central bank credit," said Rafal Chodzidlo, senior dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
At Monday's 1.1 billion zloty T-bill auction yields are expected to edge higher as banks were seen testing prices in hopes of locking in at minimum price levels, dealers said.
They said, however, that yields on the benchmark 52-week T-bill, last at 22.24 percent, would form well below secondary market levels which last amounted to around 23 percent.

Dealers said one-day cash on the money market, which traded around 24.5 percent on Friday, should rise to around the old lombard rate of 25 percent in the near-term with upcoming NBP open market operations fine-tuning rate levels.
